newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto ends Pakistan campaign with bitter attack.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto ends Pakistan campaign with bitter attack.

text.p: Ousted Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto wound up her election campaign on Saturday with a bitter attack on President Farooq Leghari, the man who sacked her on corruption charges and ordered fresh polls.
"He has brought not one corruption charge against me," Bhutto told a packed crowd in Lahore, capital of Punjab, Pakistan's most populous and influential province.
"This is the man I made president beause he wasn't strong enough to make himself chief minister of Punjab," she said.

"This is a man whose father couldn't even win a National Assembly seat and the man I made president as a reward for his hard work after he couldn't become Punjab chief minister, a man I was sure would never betray me," she said.
"Look what he's done," she said at her main rally in Lahore on the last day of campaigning for Monday's national and provincial assembly elections.

Bhutto said the dismissal of her government on November 5 was part of a plot to drive her and her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) from politics and charged again that Leghari was putting together a "King's party" to perpetuate his power.
"The PPP will not allow itself to be divided. The PPP will not allow the country to be divided," she told a dense crowd at a dusty three-way road junction in Lahore.
But even PPP officials said the crowd -- which they estimated at no more than 10,000 -- was a lot smaller than at a similar rally before the last elections three years ago.
Only in the minutes after Bhutto's helicopter flew over the junction to land in a nearby park did the crowd swell to a respectable size.

Crowd numbers are often a good barometer of election fortunes in Pakistan and Bhutto's main rival, Nawaz Sharif of the Pakistan Moslem League (PML), was expected to draw a considerably larger crowd at his last rally of the campaign on Saturday night.
Sharif, an industrialist from Lahore who has also been sacked as prime minister on corruption charges, is widely expected to regain the job.
His dismissal was overturned by the Supreme Court. By contrast, it upheld on Wednesday Leghari's action in firing Bhutto.

The latest opinion poll, by Gallup Pakistan, said the PML would win around 40 percent of the vote against around 20 percent for the PPP, although it said Bhutto's party usually added five to 10 percentage points in the last few days of campaigning.
Many analysts, however, say Sharif is likely to fall short of an overall majority in the 217-seat National Assembly and will have to look for a coalition party.
That is likely to be the Mohajir National Movement (MQM), which expects to win around a dozen seats in the southern province of Sindh, whose rural interior is Bhutto's main power base.
The MQM represents Urdu-speaking people who crossed from India to Pakistan when the old British Raj was divided on independence in 1947.
Many of them settled in Karachi, which has been the scene of ferocious violence over the past few years in which thousands of people have been killed.
The MQM, which boycotted the last elections in protest against a major crackdown on its activists, blames Bhutto for most of the violence.
One of the reasons put forward by Leghari for her dismissal, and upheld by the Supreme Court, was extra-judical killings in Karachi.

If Bhutto was sure she would lose, she showed no sign of it on Saturday in a fiery speech in which she told a responsive audience that she had improved their lives and Pakistan's standing in the world.
And, she added: "We fought terrorism in Karachi and won. Nobody else could have done that."
